📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

Industry observers note that I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged in to Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

Recent findings suggest that right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Latest York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

Sources indicate that it’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is upcoming is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

According to recent reports, the messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its people.

Industry observers note that given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

Industry observers note that finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

The Delivery Protection Act is presently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

Tech Report: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • In a recent development, sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • Sources indicate that this arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

In a recent development, sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila claims could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

Sources indicate that this arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

According to recent reports, founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The significant selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the tech giant. So using this latest material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

In a recent development, we’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the firm when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Recent findings suggest that things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced intends for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The manufacturer opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, indicates Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

It has been revealed that the glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

Industry observers note that china dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.).

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the tech giant holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our firm. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”.

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.

The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian  drones while in Russian waters.

"At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin remarked.

The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

The Border Guard later stated the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Defense Ministry remarked Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

Recent findings suggest that "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager remarked in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November.".

According to recent reports, foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the firm are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.

A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.

In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also mentioned it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider.

But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the tech giant won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation mentioned.

In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated.".

Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.

The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people stated.

Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.

The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.

Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a Newly introduced York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.

Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.

The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.

Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the manufacturer's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.

Industry observers note that frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.

Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some upcoming workers have never been fully paid, mentioned the people.

To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people stated.

At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the concern in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.

Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.

The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.

"I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the current flagship television from Sony, the Bravia 9 II, is an RGB TV model (Sony calls it “True RGB”) that brings to life even the darkest scenes in Game of Thrones. Much brighter than the midrange Bravia 7 II, the 9 II's best qualities are related to its black levels, picture quality, and excellent viewing angles that allow me to see Jon Snow and the GoT dragons perfectly, even when I'm sitting off to the side.

According to recent reports, this premium Sony television carries a premium price of $3,600 for the 65-inch model, but that’s still $1,400 less than the LG Micro RGB Evo, which retails for $5,000. I ended up preferring the overall picture quality of that LG model and some other OLED models, but—after my usual rigorous testing—I felt the Bravia 9 II came close to matching the high caliber of those other options. In fact, it’s just a notch or two lower than the absolute best television you might find.

It has been revealed that the Sony Bravia 9 II is all black, sits on two feet, and includes four HDMI ports (only two are HDMI 2.1, though, which allows for higher-bandwidth streaming and sound at 48 Gbps). Setup was a breeze; Google TV was up and running in less than five minutes, which is an impressive feat, given that both Samsung and LG televisions typically add a few extra steps to the install process, such as authenticating your login (with Samsung) or relying on an app (with the LG ThinQ).

According to recent reports, the premium Sony Bravia 9 II also offers exceptional sound. It includes two upfiring tweeters for more realistic Dolby Atmos than the Bravia 7 II, which lacks these extra channels. When I watched House of the Dragon, the room-filling audio made me feel like I was flying a dragon or piloting a ship.

According to recent reports, viewing angles on the Bravia 9 II are about the best I’ve seen on any television. I tested this element by camping out in a chair and playing video games off to the side, and there wasn’t a hint of screen glare. These perks are, again, a sign of its premium quality, verified through my usual benchmarks. Skin tones looked varied and vivid; one person had a little more red in her face than what I noticed on the LG Micro RGB Evo or the Samsung Micro RGB R95H.

In a demo-reel benchmark test I use for all televisions, I was shocked by the Bravia 9 II's stellar performance. I’ve watched the same short segment with a fence in front of a winter landscape countless times to test various models, but here, the green grass in the background looked supremely vivid and clear. It’s because the Bravia 9 II has such exceptional screen brightness, color accuracy, and absolutely no glare.

The Sony remote is just OK. I wish the Home button were centered; since it's not, I kept clicking the mic for the Google Gemini voicebot (which is in the center) by mistake. I prefer the bare-bones Samsung remote or the one included with an Apple TV 4K streaming device. Just give me a Netflix button and volume controls, and I’m good. Still, the layout of this remote mostly makes sense, and I like that it’s backlit.

Industry observers note that the Bravia 9 II didn’t pass all of my tests for performance while I watched shows and movies, but it did allow me to tweak more settings than I’m used to. For example, the TV automatically calibrated colors and tones for Spider-Man: Brand Fresh Day, but it still looked too dark. I was able to manually adjust the black level and used Vivid mode to make Spidey’s suit look extra red.

It has been revealed that however, compared to the picture quality of an OLED like the Samsung S95H, the Bravia 9 II's deep blacks looked less realistic. That's because on OLED TVs, the LEDs can be turned off entirely. The Bravia 9 II performed OK for Toy Story 5, but in darker scenes late in the film, I noticed the Samsung had inky blacks that reminded me of a high-end projector.

My main takeaway is that it's nice that you can tweak settings on the Bravia 9 II to great effect, thanks to an RGB panel that’s super-bright. The movies Awake and The Creator tested my patience a little in that regard. I adjusted the black level to precisely 61 (out of 100) and could then see faces, a predawn mountain scene, and a beach landing with better clarity. Knowing you can achieve those results is nice; actually doing it does take time.

In a recent development, while playing Resident Evil: Requiem to test brightness, picture quality, and latency, I confirmed that it's possible to adjust the black level to liven up dark scenes. I also noticed that the latency, at a 120-Hz refresh rate when I used one of the HDMI 2.1 ports, was almost nonexistent. That helped with every slight twitch when a seven-headed monster from the dark underworld of hell started attacking me.

Sources indicate that similar games, like Senua's Saga: Hellblade II, looked too gray and washed out on the midrange Bravia 7 II and some LED models I’ve tested. I also played End of Abyss, a game that takes place almost entirely in dark hallways, and the Bravia 9 II rendered those scenes with inky blacks—granted, not as black as an OLED would, but better than many LED TVs.

Sources indicate that bravia 9 II lived up to its flagship-quality promise for sportscasts, making my beloved Minnesota Vikings' purple jerseys look vivid and clear and the grass bright green—all without displaying any glare at all. News programs were bright, with strong color accuracy, but not oversaturated—a good compromise. In fact, it was so clear, I felt as if I could reach out to clip an MS Now analyst's nose hairs.

According to recent reports, the Bravia 9 II is near the top of the leaderboard of the best televisions to buy right now. You'll just want to consider the technology it uses. RGB models use red, green, and blue LEDs to create realistic colors that, in theory, improve color accuracy and vividness. Unlike an OLED TV, an RGB TV still shines those LED colors through an LCD panel. So you have to pick your poison. The Bravia 9 II looked super bright and vivid, especially during NFL games. It’s just a hair less colorful and vivid compared to the LG Micro RGB Evo.

Recent findings suggest that knowing you can tweak the settings for the results you want and that anyone in your household will be able to see America’s Got Talent from any angle in the room is a major plus. But is the Sony Bravia 9 II worth $3,600 when so many TVs cost around $2,000? I would say it depends on what you watch. I want to see dragons at night and monsters in dark hallways, but for some animated shows, sports, and network TV, you might just want your device to work well, right out of the box, without worrying about cinematic quality. Yes, a flagship lets you do a lot more, but at a much steeper price.

#70338. Latest Update: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1051 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative newly introduced possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative newly introduced possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

According to recent reports, normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Sources indicate that most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Sources indicate that pulitano notes the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

In a recent development, scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

Recent findings suggest that what’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Sources indicate that yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, notes Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano indicates long-term machine perfusion could help grow latest organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

It has been revealed that “It’s key to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” states Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

In a recent development, he’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US organization, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has mentioned it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

It has been revealed that similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

In a recent development, doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two newly introduced scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was debuted in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely upcoming.”.

#70337. Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3678 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US.
  • The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US.
  • It has been revealed that while some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

It has been revealed that while some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese company and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

According to recent reports, TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

“TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link claims.

TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

TP-Link has pledged to assemble all newly introduced routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

Some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

The Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any upcoming technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

“The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie noted in a joint statement.

The Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

Recent findings suggest that the US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”.

In a recent development, for the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security firm Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, upcoming additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List currently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

Recent findings suggest that “The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” remarked Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”.

McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

Industry observers note that “The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a firm, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”.

Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre remarked the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

McIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any firm receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft noted in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

Recent findings suggest that security expert Bruce Schneier said there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier said.

It has been revealed that with routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a fresh one. That’s the patch mechanism.”.

When asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese organization, Schneier said that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”.

TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier stated that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”.

Recent findings suggest that TP-Link states the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article remarked, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”.

TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the organization doesn’t have any new updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

Several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, mentioned in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

Industry observers note that “TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he mentioned. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese company. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”.

TP-Link noted in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”.

In 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

TP-Link’s response to Joyce remarked it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The manufacturer claims in a fact sheet that when routers provided to people by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”.

Florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”.

Last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

“Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the firm’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

“Any time a manufacturer has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” stated Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

Marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a manufacturer has larger challenges pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he said.

According to recent reports, although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a organization official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he remarked.

According to recent reports, “There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he stated. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”.

Sources indicate that kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the manufacturer’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

Kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”.

Industry observers note that kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the organization’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he said. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”.

Kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he said. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”.

Kovsky pleaded with government officials for a quick approval in a letter to the FCC last month. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”.

Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency plans if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”.

Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not currently manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound strategy to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”.

Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she said others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with on-shoring intends.

“I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she noted.

The FCC noted the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”.

Although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

After the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre noted.

Under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

According to recent reports, “We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC said in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”.

Recent findings suggest that the FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

“The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill claims.

The CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement stated the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”.

When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes.
  • Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
  • In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes.

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

The international court of justice (ICJ) noted it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.

Sources indicate that for months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.

Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.

Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.

Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.

Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.

Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.

According to recent reports, it was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.

In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.

Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.

Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.

When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.

She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.

Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.

To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.

It has been revealed that elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.

His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

Recent findings suggest that alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

#70334. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1942 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Tech giant insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on customers and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” stated Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

Recent findings suggest that the revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

Recent findings suggest that there is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any organization operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly people until the end of 2018, the year it listed in Fresh York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the firm set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the firm only targeted owners in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they mentioned.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it noted it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

Industry observers note that the app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers mentioned.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they remarked.

According to recent reports, in China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

According to recent reports, “I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

It has been revealed that toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

Recent findings suggest that according to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to consumers’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he stated.

In a recent development, of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews indicated that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

In a recent development, suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread swiftly among other researchers, who did name the manufacturer. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new patch of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the upgrade, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

Sources indicate that the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the tech giant’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to substantial data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source mentioned.

Industry observers note that most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the upgrade, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

It has been revealed that the Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

Industry observers note that the ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

According to recent reports, “Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A gun battle between Mexican soldiers and alleged gang members in the city of Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa, ended with special forces detaining senior members of the Beltran Leyva drug trafficking network, Mexican officials noted on Saturday.

The gang is aligned with the Mayos, one of the factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Authorities stated the overnight raid resulted in the capture of the suspected drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza F., better known as "Chapo Isidro," who is believed to be the leader of Beltran Leyva.

In a recent development, the operation left at least 11 people dead. Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed, Mexico’s Defense Ministry said on Saturday afternoon.

Recent findings suggest that the 44-year-old Mexican national is one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives. The US law enforcement agency claims his group is responsible for smuggling "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States," and has offered a $5 million (€4.56 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.

He is also wanted in Mexico on charges including organized crime. "Chapo Isidro" was once a rival of imprisoned drug kingpin Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman.

The three detainees were transported to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military remarked.

It was not immediately clear whether authorities would extradite "Chapo Isidro" to the US.

Industry observers note that on Saturday, Mexican authorities said the raid was conducted due to "intelligence coordination" between Mexico's military and US agencies. However, they offered few details about how authorities in both countries coordinated.

In a post on X, US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wrote: "Results like these are not achieved overnight. They are the product of sustained cooperation and trust. This is what we can accomplish when we work together. ​We will continue pursuing criminals.".

The troops used "stealth and surprise" to reach the area, establishing a perimeter around the drug dealer's location and then moving in from multiple directions, according to Mexico's US embassy.

According to recent reports, unverified videos from Guasave, however, revealed military helicopters firing at ground targets and sports fans scrambling for safety during a baseball game. Some of the violence in the western Mexican city seems to have taken place after "Chapo Isidro" was arrested, with drug cartels attempting to retaliate against the authorities and civilians for the move.

Mexico's Defense Ministry confirmed cartel members set up roadblocks in the area, but added that security forces were assisting local authorities in restoring order.

Industry observers note that the Guasave raid is only the latest in a string of high-profile moves against senior leaders of Mexico's illegal drug trade​​​​​​. Less than two weeks ago, the Mexican Navy declared the arrest of Rafael A., suspected of leading a cartel cell active in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.

Mexican President ​Claudia Sheinbaum is facing pressure from Donald Trump, who has threatened to take military action against cartels on Mexican territory.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

Nintendo Store — Out of stock right now, but you can add it to your wishlist to get pinged the second a restock hits.

Amazon — Dropping tiny batches of consoles randomly throughout the day.
